analysis.one_liner: Restores the Glass-Steagall wall separating commercial banking from investment banking and securities firms.
analysis.headline: The bill to restore the Glass-Steagall separation of banking and securities never got a hearing or vote; it was referred to the House Financial Services Committee in December 2009 and died there when the Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rebuilt the Glass-Steagall wall that stood from 1933 until 1999, when the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act allowed banks that hold insured deposits to merge with investment banks and securities firms. It would have barred banks from affiliating with securities firms, barred securities executives from sitting on bank boards, and given existing combinations two years to unwind. It would also have stopped regulators from narrowing the prohibition by interpretation. The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and received no further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary bank depositors and taxpayers: insured deposits would no longer back securities businesses whose losses could require taxpayer-funded bailouts. It also benefits traditional banks that keep to deposit-taking and lending, since they would no longer compete against combines of insured deposits and securities trading, and reduces systemic risk from 'too big to fail' combinations.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Depositors, taxpayers, and plain commercial banks

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits insured depository institutions (banks that hold federally insured deposits) from affiliating with brokers, dealers, investment advisers, investment companies, or securities underwriters.

Bars officers, directors, and employees of securities firms from simultaneously serving on bank boards, with a narrow exception where a banking agency finds no undue influence, and requires current dual-serving individuals to quit within 60 days.
Gives banks and bank holding companies two years to wind down prohibited affiliations in an orderly way, with limited extensions.

Locks the prohibition in by ratifying the Supreme Court's interpretation in Investment Company Institute v. Camp and barring banking agencies and courts from construing it more narrowly than the Court did.
Requires banking regulators to report to Congress each time they grant an exception or extension to the separation rules.

analysis.who_pays: Large universal banks and financial conglomerates (such as those formed under Gramm-Leach-Bliley) bear the cost: they would have to divest securities affiliates or banking operations within two years. Securities firms lose access to insured deposits and bank funding. Some economists argue that forcing the split could raise costs for consumers and that bank-securities combinations were not the principal cause of the 2008 crisis (the crisis also came from mortgage lending, derivatives, and the shadow banking system outside Glass-Steagall's repeal).
analysis.who_pays_short: Large bank-securities conglomerates and securities firms

drawbacks.text: Unwinding conglomerates within two years is a major restructuring that could impose costs on banks and potentially on customers of combined services; some financial economists argue that Glass-Steagall's repeal was not the main cause of the 2008 crisis, since the failures (Lehman, AIG, Bear Stearns) were concentrated in investment banks and insurers not covered by Glass-Steagall, so restoration might not prevent a future crisis and could put U.S. banks at a competitive disadvantage against foreign universal banks.

Repealing 'financial subsidiaries' and financial holding company powers would strip banks of some diversification benefits, and economists have argued diversification can actually reduce bank failure risk, so the cost-benefit is genuinely debated rather than one-sided.
The bill was introduced with only two cosponsors and received no committee action, so it had no realistic path to becoming law, meaning any real-world costs or benefits were moot.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would restore a major Depression-era structural safeguard that had protected insured deposits from securities losses for 66 years. Its benefit is reduced taxpayer exposure to bank failures caused by securities losses and reduced concentration in banking. The costs are real: forced divestitures within two years, possible loss of diversification benefits, and honest disagreement among economists about how much the 1999 repeal contributed to the 2008 crisis (key failures were at investment banks and insurers the law never covered). It was a broad, sweeping repeal rather than a targeted fix, and it never received committee review where these tradeoffs could have been examined.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on the day it was introduced, never received a hearing or markup, and died there when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Rep. Marcy Kaptur (D-OH) introduced the bill on December 16, 2009, over a year after the financial crisis peaked.
It was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day and never received any further action.
It drew only two cosponsors, both House Democrats, in a chamber where Democrats held 253 of 431 seats.
The bill died when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, without a hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large bank-securities conglomerates and securities firms: the existing combinations of insured deposits and securities businesses created under Gramm-Leach-Bliley were left fully intact, and Congress instead enacted the narrower Dodd-Frank financial regulation in 2010 rather than restoring the full Glass-Steagall separation.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big universal banks; the Gramm-Leach-Bliley status quo survived

for.name: Marcy Kaptur
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 16, 2009, to restore the Glass-Steagall separation between commercial banking and securities firms.

for.name: 2 of 253 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsors joined.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and took no further action—no hearing, markup, or vote—letting it die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Democratic sponsor and two Democratic cosponsors with no Republican support shown in the record; it never reached a vote, so no party-split vote occurred, and majority-party House Democrats did not advance it.

industries.industry: Large universal banks and financial conglomerates (e.g., combines of commercial banking with securities businesses formed under Gramm-Leach-Bliley)
industries.note: The bill would have forced them to divest either their insured-deposit banking operations or their securities and investment-banking affiliates within two years, unwinding the business model Gramm-Leach-Bliley made legal. The status quo that persisted instead keeps insured deposits connected to securities businesses whose losses can create taxpayer-backed bailouts and 'too big to fail' firms.

industries.industry: Securities firms, brokers, dealers, and investment advisers
industries.note: They would lose access to affiliation with insured depositories, and their executives would be barred from bank boards. Their interest in keeping the status quo runs against depositors' interest in having insured deposits isolated from securities risk.

industries.industry: Traditional plain commercial banks without securities operations
industries.note: Removing securities-business combinations would reduce competition from conglomerates using insured deposits in securities activities and reduce systemic bailout risk that these banks could otherwise be drawn into funding. (Inference from the bill's structural effect rather than a specific source.)
